1.pericope_label: Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush,

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the verse as the title of the first list and reads its closing subscription, explains that the brethren of the priests are the Levites, connects the twenty-two heads named here both to the priestly houses listed further down and to the fifteen who sealed the covenant, and identifies the last Levite named as the Asaphite head of the first band of singers.

Gill states the terms of the register — priests and Levites who came up from Babylon with Zerubbabel the prince and Jeshua the high priest — notes that the priestly names run through the next six verses, and observes that the names of the second verse stand among the sealers of the covenant, one of them appearing later in an altered form.

Henry asks why a register of names is here at all and answers that it keeps these men in remembrance, so that later generations might know to whom under God they owed the revival of their religion; he adds a second purpose, to stir up the sons who inherited these offices to imitate their fathers, and cautions that the Jeremiah and Ezra named near the head of the list are probably neither the prophet nor the scribe.

themes: Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra,
Amariah, Malluch, Hattush,

6.pericope_label: Shemaiah, and Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua. Moreover the Levites: Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, which was over the thanksgiving, he and his brethren. Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches. And Jeshua begat Joiakim, Joiakim also begat Eliashib, and Eliashib begat Joiada, And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua. And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah; Of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan; Of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the conjunction before one name as marking off those who did not seal the covenant, insists the men are chief genealogically rather than by course, since the courses are complete in none of the lists, and declines to explain the anomalies between the two registers; Delitzsch reads the inserted genealogy as a connecting link that dates the lists on either side of it by the high priest then in office, and takes the pair named after the Levites as an answering choir rather than a watch.

Gill counts twenty heads in the son's days against twenty-two in the father's and accounts for the difference by two houses that left no descendants; on the high-priestly succession he reports the identification of the last name with the Jaddus of Josephus who met Alexander, and concludes from it that the paragraph cannot be Nehemiah's but was inserted later by a godly hand under divine direction.

Clarke gives the courses their history, twenty-four orders established by David and continuing until the Romans destroyed Jerusalem; Wesley describes the office over the thanksgiving as a duty rather than a rank, to see that the psalms of thanksgiving were sung continually at the due time and in the due manner, and explains the second register as sons serving in their fathers' places.

debates.question: Who wrote the note on the high-priestly succession?

positions.position: Not Nehemiah: if the last high priest named is the one who met Alexander, Nehemiah could not have lived so long, so a later hand inserted the fragment.
It belongs where it stands, as a connecting link explaining how the lists on either side are dated.

22.pericope_label: The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian. The sons of Levi, the chief of the fathers, were written in the book of the chronicles, even until the days of Johanan the son of Eliashib. And the chief of the Levites: Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua the son of Kadmiel, with their brethren over against them, to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God, ward over against ward. Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates. These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe.

schools.summary: Delitzsch strikes out as a gloss the word making one Levitical head the son of another, notes that the phrase ward over against ward is borrowed from the gatekeepers and applied here to the choirs, and marks the final verse as the subscription covering both lists; Ellicott observes that the account resumes with a list of the temple's serving officers, many of the names already familiar.

Gill identifies the third high priest of the second temple, notes that some refer the book of chronicles mentioned here to a particular passage, marks where the thread of Nehemiah's own narrative resumes after the two intervening verses, and dates the closing subscription by a high priest whose grandfather had held the office in Babylon.

Clarke tells the story attached to the last name — the priest going out in his robes to meet Alexander, who spared the city, bowed before him, worshipped at the temple and granted many privileges — reports without resolving the dispute over which Darius is meant, and denies flatly that the book of chronicles named here can be the canonical book of that name; Wesley takes the earlier Darius and draws the consequence, that this Jaddua may be the father of the man who met Alexander rather than the man himself.

debates.question: Which Darius does the chapter reach?

positions.position: The later king, defeated by Alexander — so the chapter reaches to the very end of the Persian period.
The earlier king of that name, which makes the Jaddua named here the father of the man who met Alexander.

themes: The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian.
The sons of Levi, the chief of the fathers, were written in the book of the chronicles, even until the days of Johanan the son of Eliashib.

27.pericope_label: And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps. And the sons of the singers gathered themselves together, both out of the plain country round about Jerusalem, and from the villages of Netophathi; Also from the house of Gilgal, and out of the fields of Geba and Azmaveth: for the singers had builded them villages round about Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets the dedication in the book's sequence, after the measures for filling the city had been carried out, explains that the Levites had to be fetched in because only some lived in Jerusalem, proposes a correction to the awkward phrase about dedication and joy, and reads the region the singers came from as the southern Jordan valley rather than the neighbourhood of the city; Ellicott places them instead in villages to the north.

Gill suggests the register was set down because so many priests and Levites took part in the dedication, widens what was dedicated to the whole city with its gates and houses, argues from the lesser to the greater that a new city deserved what a new house received, and passes on the tradition that the day was afterwards kept annually.
Clarke identifies one of the singers' settlements as the village raised where Israel encamped after crossing Jordan under Joshua.

Henry hears the contrast with the earlier chapters — the wall built in fear and trembling, dedicated in joy and triumph — and gives the ceremony two meanings: a thanksgiving for a work finished against opposition, and a devoting of the city to God in his own name, the builders acknowledging that they held it as his tenants.

positions.position: In the southern Jordan valley near Jericho, and in villages some miles to the south-west.
Chiefly in villages to the north of the city.

themes: And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps.

30.pericope_label: And the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and purified the people, and the gates, and the wall. Then I brought up the princes of Judah upon the wall, and appointed two great companies of them that gave thanks, whereof one went on the right hand upon the wall toward the dung gate: And after them went Hoshaiah, and half of the princes of Judah,

schools.summary: Ellicott states the principle that consecration must be preceded by cleansing, and makes the gates and the wall purified by sprinkling as the ministers were by offering and ablution; Delitzsch reads the princes of Judah as the princes of the whole community and describes the two thanksgiving companies going opposite ways along the wall to halt facing each other at the house of God, noting that the word for thanksgiving passes from praise to thankoffering and so to a company of singers.

Gill takes the purification to have been by washing of bodies and clothes, perhaps with the sprinkling of the water of purification, observes that the wall was broad enough to be walked along, holds that the princes of Benjamin are included under the name of Judah, and notes that the second half of the princes followed with Hoshaiah at their head.

Clarke describes a wider discipline of washings and abstinence, and makes the cleansing of the gates and wall a matter of clearing filth and rubbish rather than of rite; Wesley turns the verse into a charge, that those who would sanctify others must first sanctify themselves with purity of mind and sincerity of intention.

debates.question: How were the gates and the wall purified?

positions.position: By clearing them: nothing was needed but to remove the filth from the gates and the rubbish from against the wall.
By sprinkling, as the ministers themselves were purified by offerings and ablutions.

themes: And the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and purified the people, and the gates, and the wall.

33.pericope_label: And Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam, Judah, and Benjamin, and Shemaiah, and Jeremiah, And certain of the priests’ sons with trumpets; namely, Zechariah the son of Jonathan, the son of Shemaiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Michaiah, the son of Zaccur, the son of Asaph: And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them. And at the fountain gate, which was over against them, they went up by the stairs of the city of David, at the going up of the wall, above the house of David, even unto the water gate eastward.

schools.summary: Ellicott suspects one of the names simply duplicates the one before it and finds the arrangement of the company odd, with the laity set between priests before and behind; Delitzsch puts the trumpeters at seven on the evidence of a later verse, counts eight musicians following their head, and traces the route from the dung gate to the fountain gate and up by the stairs of the city of David to the water gate, while admitting that the description as a whole is not quite intelligible.

Gill distinguishes the Ezra named among the princes from Ezra the scribe, who has his own place later in the procession, insists that Judah and Benjamin here are two men rather than two tribes on the authority of Jarchi, notes that the trumpets were sounded by the priests, and fixes the fountain gate to the south of the dung gate.

themes: And Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam,
Judah, and Benjamin, and Shemaiah, and Jeremiah,

38.pericope_label: And the other company of them that gave thanks went over against them, and I after them, and the half of the people upon the wall, from beyond the tower of the furnaces even unto the broad wall; And from above the gate of Ephraim, and above the old gate, and above the fish gate, and the tower of Hananeel, and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate: and they stood still in the prison gate. So stood the two companies of them that gave thanks in the house of God, and I, and the half of the rulers with me:

schools.summary: Delitzsch follows the northern route through its named towers and gates to the halt at the prison gate; Ellicott observes that the gate of Ephraim is missing from the account of the repairs, having survived in reasonable condition with part of the broad wall, and distinguishes the companies standing outside from their later entry to present offerings, judging the day's main interest to have lain in worship under the open sky.

Gill gives the second company's direction as leftward along the northern wall, explains the gate of Ephraim by the road it opened toward that tribe's old territory, and notes that the two processions met in the great court of the temple, no smaller space being able to hold them.

Wesley attends to the halt rather than the route: the company stood still and waited, as their brethren waited, so that the two might enter together in due order and complete the solemnity as one body.

41.pericope_label: And the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets; And Maaseiah, and Shemaiah, and Eleazar, and Uzzi, and Jehohanan, and Malchijah, and Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer. Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that these priestly names, like the earlier ones in the procession, are personal and are not found in any of the registers filling the first half of the chapter, and holds the order of the closing verse to be its point: it is full of joy, but the abundant offering of sacrifice comes before the rejoicing.

Gill notes that these priests stood with the rest and that the eight names following them seem all to be of trumpeters, reads the great sacrifices as many sacrifices after Ben Melech, supposes them of the larger cattle, and observes that the peace offerings among them were feasted on by the people, which made the day a festival.

Wesley fastens on the children rejoicing with the rest, whose hosannas were not despised but are recorded to their praise, and draws the rule that all who share in public mercies ought to join in public thanksgivings.

themes: And the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;
And Maaseiah, and Shemaiah, and Eleazar, and Uzzi, and Jehohanan, and Malchijah, and Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer.

Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off.

44.pericope_label: And at that time were some appointed over the chambers for the treasures, for the offerings, for the firstfruits, and for the tithes, to gather into them out of the fields of the cities the portions of the law for the priests and Levites: for Judah rejoiced for the priests and for the Levites that waited. And both the singers and the porters kept the ward of their God, and the ward of the purification, according to the commandment of David, and of Solomon his son.

schools.summary: Delitzsch credits the joint labours of Nehemiah and Ezra with restoring the law's enactments for the conduct and upkeep of public worship, supplies the subject of the clause about the wards from the opening of the verse, and makes two textual repairs — a conjunction wanting before one royal name and another standing superfluously in the next verse; Ellicott divides the sentence the same way, so that the clause covers the whole ministry, and defines keeping the ward as observing the appointed times and seasons of sacrifice and thanksgiving.

Gill fixes the appointments to the day of the dedication itself, while the people were still in the frame the service had put them in, and describes the overseers chosen to keep the treasuries and see that what came in went to its intended use; on the wards he takes the plain reading, that the singers kept their courses and the porters kept the gates against anything unclean.
Wesley reads the ward as that charge which God had prescribed, and in particular the charge of purification, that no unclean person or thing should enter the house or its courts.

Henry treats these verses as a test applied to the thanksgiving itself: when such a day leaves ministers and people more careful and more cheerful in their duty afterwards, it has been accepted of God, and the joy that engages us to duty and enlarges us in it proves itself.

debates.question: Whose wards does the verse describe?

positions.position: The singers and the porters, each keeping the duty of his own office.
The priests and Levites kept the ward, and the singers and porters theirs as well, the clause covering the whole ministry.

themes: And at that time were some appointed over the chambers for the treasures, for the offerings, for the firstfruits, and for the tithes, to gather into them out of the fields of the cities the portions of the law for the priests and Levites: for Judah rejoiced for the priests and for the Levites that waited.

46.pericope_label: For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God. And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel, and in the days of Nehemiah, gave the portions of the singers and the porters, every day his portion: and they sanctified holy things unto the Levites; and the Levites sanctified them unto the children of Aaron.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the phrase of old the reverence these chapters consistently show for ancient precedent, and describes the chain of maintenance in a sentence, the Levites standing between people and priests, receiving the tithe and paying over a tithe of the tithe.

Gill explains the appeal to the old days as an appeal to office, chiefs of the singers being set over the rest to instruct them and see the work done properly, and reads the closing verse as a tribute to two administrations under which the Levites were paid their dues punctually and at the proper season.

Clarke sets out the mechanism — singers and porters supported by the people at large, each receiving his portion daily, the sacred things delivered by the people to the Levites and by them presented to the priests — and stops on the word for that transaction, sanctifying meaning here to dedicate a thing to the use for which it was designed rather than to perform a ceremony over it.

themes: For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God.

And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel, and in the days of Nehemiah, gave the portions of the singers and the porters, every day his portion: and they sanctified holy things unto the Levites; and the Levites sanctified them unto the children of Aaron.
